PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC10292167  PMID: 37378133 Abstract While radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have long been used in the assessment of osteoarthritis (OA), ultrasound imaging has been rapidly accepted by musculoskeletal providers in both the assessment and treatment of OA. figures.caption: Figure 1. Anterior Evaluation, Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 1A : The patient is placed in a supine with a bolster under the posterior knee to flex the knee to 30˚. The probe is aligned parallel to the quadriceps tendon. Figure 1B : The quadriceps tendon (1), quadriceps fat pad (2), suprapatellar recess (3), prefemoral fat pad (4), femur (5) and patella (6) are identified.

Figure 2. Long Axis View of Anterior Knee in the Setting of Osteoarthritis. Open in a new tab Ultrasound image of a knee with osteoarthritis demonstrating hypoechoic effusion (star) and synovitis (bracket).

Figure 3. Anterior Evaluation, Short Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 3A : The probe is rotated 90˚ perpendicular to the quadriceps tendon. Figure 3B : The quadriceps tendon (1), quadriceps fat pad (2), suprapatellar recess (3), prefemoral fat pad (4), and femur (5) are identified.

Figure 4. Short Axis View of Anterior Knee in the Setting of Osteoarthritis. Open in a new tab Ultrasound image findings that support the diagnosis of osteoarthritis are synovitis (bracket) and hypoechoic effusion (star).

Figure 5. Anterior Evaluation, Maximal Knee Flexion. Open in a new tab Figure 5A : The knee is placed in maximal flexion with the probe aligned 90˚ perpendicular to the quadriceps tendon. Figure 5B : The quadriceps tendon (1), hyaline cartilage (2) and femur (3) are identified [ 12 ].
Figure 6. Anterior Evaluation, Maximal Knee Flexion in the Setting of Osteoarthritis. Open in a new tab Ultrasound image demonstrating loss of hyaline cartilage (bracket).

Figure 7. Anterior Evaluation of Medial Cartilage. Open in a new tab Figure 7A : The probe is positioned medially in longitudinal access over the medial femoral condyle. Figure 7B : The hyaline cartilage (1) and femur (2) are identified.
Figure 8. Long Axis View of Medial Condyle in the Setting of Osteoarthritis. Open in a new tab Ultrasound image which demonstrates loss of cartilage thickness and cortical irregularities (bracket).

Figure 9. Anterior Evaluation of Lateral Cartilage. Open in a new tab Figure 9A : The probe is positioned laterally in longitudinal access over the lateral femoral condyle. Figure 9B : The hyaline cartilage (1) and femur (2) are identified.

Figure 10. Medial Evaluation, Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 10A : The knee is repositioned in 30˚ of flexion and the probe is positioned over the medial joint line with the distal aspect of the probe over the proximal tibia. Figure 10B : The distal femur (1), medial meniscus (2), proximal tibia (3), and medial collateral ligament (4) are identified.

Figure 11. Lateral Evaluation, Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 11A : The knee remains in 30˚ of flexion and the probe is positioned over the lateral joint line with the distal aspect of the probe over the proximal tibia. Figure 11B : The distal femur (1), lateral meniscus (2), and proximal tibia (3) are identified.
Figure 12. Lateral Evaluation, Long Axis View in the Setting of Osteoarthritis. Open in a new tab Ultrasound image demonstrating an osteophyte (arrow) on the lateral condyle.

Figure 13. Posteriormedial Evaluation, Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 13A : The probe is placed over the medial aspect of the popliteal fossa in a longitudinal axis. Figure 13B : The semimembranosus (1), medial head of gastrocnemius (2), presence of a baker’s cyst (3), medial femoral condyle (4), and hyaline cartilage (5) are identified.

Figure 14. Posteriorlateral Evaluation, Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 14A : The probe is placed over the lateral aspect of the popliteal fossa in a longitudinal axis. Figure 14B : The semitendinosus (1), lateral head of gastrocnemius (2), lateral femoral condyle hyaline cartilage (3), and lateral proximal tibia (4) are identified.

Figure 15. Posteromedial Evaluation, Long Axis View in the Setting of Knee Osteoarthritis. Open in a new tab Ultrasound image which demonstrates a needle (arrow) aspirating a hypoechoic fluid collection (Baker’s Cyst) between the semimembranosus (star) and medial head of the gastrocnemius (bracket).

Figure 16. Standing Medial Knee, Extended Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 16A : The probe is placed over the medial knee joint while the patient is standing, and the knee is extended. Figure 16B : MCL (1), medial meniscus (2), medial femoral condyle (3), and proximal tibia (4) are identified. MCL: medial collateral ligament

Figure 17. Standing Medial Knee, Flexed Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 17A : The probe is placed over the medial knee joint while the patient is standing, and the knee is flexed. Figure 17B : MCL (1), medial meniscus (2), medial femoral condyle (3), and proximal tibia (4) are identified. MCL: medial collateral ligament

Figure 18. Standing Lateral knee, Extended Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 18A : The probe is placed over the lateral knee joint while the patient is standing with the knee extended. Figure 18B : Biceps femoris (1), lateral femoral condyle (2), lateral meniscus (3), and proximal tibia (4) are identified.

Figure 19. Standing Lateral Knee, Flexed Long Axis View. Open in a new tab Figure 19A : The probe is placed over the lateral knee joint while the patient is standing with the knee flexed. Figure 19B : Lateral femoral condyle (1), lateral meniscus (2), and proximal tibia (3) are identified.
